TECHNICAL INFORMATION LETTER
7F AND 9F AFT END COMPRESSOR RUBS
APPLICATION
All 7F and 9F Heavy Duty Gas Turbines
PURPOSE
To inform users to monitor equipment operation and condition, and to identify the onset, occurrence, and effects of aft end compressor rubs (when the tip of the rotor blade rubs the casing).  Rubs are evident when blade tip material is adversely affected. Information in this TIL is supplemental to information in the Inspection and Maintenance Manual provided with the gas turbine.
REASON FOR REVISION
To update the technical content of the TIL, including frequency of tip loss and recommendations when discovered.
Compliance Category

TIL 1502-2R1
BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The compressor section of F-Class gas turbines has 18
(0-17) stages of rotating components (rotor blades) and
stationary components (stator vanes).
Some F-class machines have experienced aft end compressor rubs. These rubs range from light scoring on the casing to material loss at the blade tip. This phenomenon was concluded to be very low risk relative to unit operation and reliability. No performance impact and no forced outages have been experienced as a result. Rotor blades in rows 13, 14, and 15 are primarily affected.
Figure 1: F-Class Compressor Cross-Section
Based on the conclusion of Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and fleet experience, aft end rubs are primarily induced because of frequent restarts between two (2) to eight (8) hours after shutdown. During this transient period, the thermal compression of the casing relative to the rotor can decrease clearances and can lead to rubs upon restart. The heat generated from a rub can lower the local material fatigue strength of the blade resulting in material tip loss in the event of another rub. Typical material loss dimensions are less than 1/16 inch² in area (see Figure 2).
Typical Tip Loss
1/4"
Figure 2: Typical Blade Tip Loss
Restarting a unit 2 to 8 hours after a shutdown or trip is within the operating envelope, but this may cause rubs in some cases. Aft end rubs and/or tip loss pose very low risk to unit operation and reliability. No performance impact and no forced outages have been experienced due to this issue.
RECOMMENDATIONS
Follow operating practices per GER 3620 to reduce the potential for rubs on aft end compressor blades. In addition to the GER 3620 guidelines, the following recommendations would also help minimize aft end rubs and tip loss occurrence.
Keep enclosure doors closed during startup, shutdown and normal operation.
Be aware that restarting the gas turbine between two (2) and eight (8) hours following a shutdown or trip will cause the clearances in the aft end to decrease. If the unit operates this way now or has in the past, there is a potential for this clearance closure to cause aft end tip rubs. As a result, the area should be included in the yearly borescope inspections.
• Eliminate any potential pipe leaks that may cause quenching of the gas turbine compressor discharge casing.
Ensure vent fans and exhaust fans to the gas turbine enclosure are functioning properly such that no local forced convection is taking place at or near the compressor discharge casing.
Integrate the inspection for aft end compressor rubs with your yearly scheduled borescope inspection per GER 3620. Observe rotor blade stages 13 through 17 and look for mushroomed material (see Figure 3), bluing at the blade tip, and / or markings in the casing area.
Casing
Mushrooming Material Tip
Rotating Airfoil
Figure 3: Fractured Tip Surface

If rubs or tip loss do occur, blending to increase clearances can be performed at Major Inspections (MI) or when the Compressor Discharge Casing (CDC) is removed. During repairs, clearances of rotor blades can be increased radially by tip grinding and polishing, and tip corners repaired by blade blending. Typically, 20 mils radially of material can be removed to both increase clearance and remove heat affected and rolled over material.
Following this operation, a penetrant inspection must be performed to ensure no tip cracks are present. If the CDC is removed prior to the major inspection, clearances can also be increased to eliminate the potential for tip rubs should the customer desire. Please contact your local GE service representative for assistance.

BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The function of the turbine rotor in a heavy-duty gas turbine engine includes carrying turbine blade loads, transmitting torque to the compressor and generator for power generation, as well as supplying the turbine blades with cooling air.
Prior to assembly, the individual disks or wheels are balanced by the addition of weights installed in a groove. The weights are held in place by deforming the metal on either the balance weight or the balance weight groove. The turbine blades are retained axially by a snap ring type lock wire that is located in a machined groove passing through the turbine blades and turbine wheel.  The portion of the wheel retaining the lock wire is known as the lock wire tab.  The F-class turbine blade cooling air supply is provided through cooling slots in the bottom of the stage 1 and 2 turbine wheel dovetails.

The disks in the turbine rotor are made of a high nickel alloy that is sensitive to surface imperfections where an intergranular crack may initiate and propagate due to high stresses and temperatures. Depending on the initiation location, an undetected crack may continue to propagate due to exposure to stress and temperature until either:
1- the crack is detected and either repaired or the rotor is removed from service, or
2- the crack propagates to a critical length, releasing a wheel section and/or adjacent turbine blades into the turbine hot gas path section potentially resulting in significant damage.

Continuous improvements have been made to the turbine rotor wheels over time in order to improve their overall damage sensitivity.
Rotors operating in high ambient and humid or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation. Recommended inspections and inspection intervals to help mitigate crack propagation are provided based on wheel features, such as: shot peening condition at first fire, cooling slot geometry, material heat treatment, and environmental conditions. In some cases, rotors may be swapped from site to site in order to expedite an outage. This TIL is being issued to all general F-Class turbine rotors in order to provide recommendations for the various configurations. Rotors operating in high ambient and/or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation and are addressed in TIL 1937.
Shot Peening Effect
Early generation turbine rotors have the highest sensitivity to surface imperfections. These rotors were manufactured and fired without full shot peen coverage of the turbine wheels. Shot peening leaves a residual compressive stress and decreases the risk of initiating a crack. Wheels that operated without shot peening have an increased risk of initiating and propagating a crack in the rim region of the turbine rotor and in the turbine wheel dovetail slots. After 1996, all F-class turbine wheels shipped with full peening coverage; these wheels were never fired without shot peening.
Cooling Slot
During operation, the intersection of the cooling slot and dovetail slot is subjected to high temperatures and tensile stresses caused by turbine blade pull. The high temperatures and stresses in conjunction with an adverse edge condition have been known to initiate cracks in this location.

BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
A gas turbine rotor is an assembly of shafts, wheels, disks, and spacers. A means of balance is incorporated into each of these rotor components and the various assemblies. A balance weight groove (BWG) is one example of a feature that is used to provide a means of balancing. The BWG is an annular channel that is machined into a rotor component that provides a location for weights to be installed for balance purposes on either the piece part or as a rotor assembly. This annular channel may contain two BWG entry slots, as shown in Figure 1, located approximately 180 degrees apart that allow for the balance weights to be easily installed and located in the appropriate locations on the wheel or shaft.
Figure 1: BWG Entry Slots - Correct Machining
During non-destructive evaluation (NDE) of a distance piece (DP) as part of a rotor life extension (RLE), a crack-like indication was observed in the corner of a balance weight groove entry slot. Both grooves on the specific part showed similar indications as depicted in Figure 2. GE has inspected additional parts with similar features and observed similar indication findings.
Figure 2: Indications Found on DP During RLE - Observed Machining Issue
Upon completion of a root cause investigation, GE determined the cause is associated with the variation in the corner condition of the balance weight groove entry slots and interactions with the various stresses during gas turbine start-up, shutdown, and loaded operation (gravity sag, etc). Depending upon the specific nature of a units operation and the specific condition of the part slot corner, crack-like indications may form over the lifetime of the component. If these crack-like indications propagate to a large enough size, it may be possible for continued rapid crack growth to occur associated with gravity sag related bending of the rotor as it rotates (high cycle fatigue related mechanism). If not mitigated, the fracture propagation may lead the CAS and/or DP to separate into two separate pieces. Separation of either shaft into two pieces may create the possibility for components to exit the gas turbine leading to the possibility for INJURY TO PERSONNEL/INDIVIDUALS and substantial damage to adjacent equipment.

BACKGROUND DISCUSSION

Prior to assembly, the individual disks or wheels are balanced by the addition of weights installed in a groove.  The weights are held in place by deforming the metal on either the balance weight or the balance weight groove. The turbine blades are retained axially by a snap ring type lock wire that is located in a machined groove passing through the turbine blades and turbine wheel.  The portion of the wheel retaining the lock wire is known as the lock wire tab.  The F-class turbine blade cooling air supply is provided through cooling slots in the bottom of the stage 1 and 2 turbine wheel dovetails.

The disks in the turbine rotor are made of a high nickel alloy that is sensitive to surface imperfections where an intergranular crack may initiate and propagate due to high stresses and temperatures. Depending on the initiation location, an undetected crack may continue to propagate due to exposure to stress and temperature until either: 1- the crack is detected and either repaired or the rotor is removed from service, or 2- the crack propagates to a critical length, releasing a wheel section and/or adjacent turbine blades into the turbine hot gas path section potentially resulting in significant damage. Continuous improvements have been made to the turbine rotor wheels over time in order to improve their overall damage sensitivity.
Rotors operating in high ambient and humid or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation.
Recommended inspections and inspection intervals to mitigate crack propagation are provided based on wheel features, such as shot peening condition at first fire, cooling slot geometry, material heat treatment, and environmental conditions.  In some cases, rotors may be swapped from site to site in order to expedite an outage. Shot Peening Effect
Early generation turbine rotors have the highest sensitivity to surface imperfections. These rotors were manufactured and fired without full shot peen coverage of the turbine wheels. Shot peening leaves a residual compressive stress and decreases the risk of initiating a crack. Wheels that operated without shot peening have an increased risk of initiating and propagating a crack in the rim region of the turbine rotor and in the turbine wheel dovetail slots. After 1996, all F-class turbine wheels shipped with full peening coverage; these wheels were never fired without shot peening.
Cooling Slot
During operation, the intersection of the cooling slot and dovetail slot is subjected to high temperatures and tensile stresses caused by turbine blade pull.  The high temperatures and stresses in conjunction with an adverse edge condition have been known to initiate cracks in this location.

TECHNICAL INFORMATION LETTER
7F AND 9F AFT END COMPRESSOR RUBS
APPLICATION
All 7F and 9F Heavy Duty Gas Turbines
PURPOSE
To inform users to monitor equipment operation and condition, and to identify the onset, occurrence, and effects of aft end compressor rubs (when the tip of the rotor blade rubs the casing).  Rubs are evident when blade tip material is adversely affected. Information in this TIL is supplemental to information in the Inspection and Maintenance Manual provided with the gas turbine.
REASON FOR REVISION
To update the technical content of the TIL, including frequency of tip loss and recommendations when discovered.

BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The compressor section of F-Class gas turbines has 18
(0-17) stages of rotating components (rotor blades) and
stationary components (stator vanes).
Some F-class machines have experienced aft end compressor rubs. These rubs range from light scoring on the casing to material loss at the blade tip. This phenomenon was concluded to be very low risk relative to unit operation and reliability. No performance impact and no forced outages have been experienced as a result. Rotor blades in rows 13, 14, and 15 are primarily affected.
Figure 1: F-Class Compressor Cross-Section
Based on the conclusion of Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and fleet experience, aft end rubs are primarily induced because of frequent restarts between two (2) to eight (8) hours after shutdown. During this transient period, the thermal compression of the casing relative to the rotor can decrease clearances and can lead to rubs upon restart. The heat generated from a rub can lower the local material fatigue strength of the blade resulting in material tip loss in the event of another rub. Typical material loss dimensions are less than 1/16 inch² in area (see Figure 2).
Typical Tip Loss
1/4"
Figure 2: Typical Blade Tip Loss
Restarting a unit 2 to 8 hours after a shutdown or trip is within the operating envelope, but this may cause rubs in some cases. Aft end rubs and/or tip loss pose very low risk to unit operation and reliability. No performance impact and no forced outages have been experienced due to this issue.
RECOMMENDATIONS
Follow operating practices per GER 3620 to reduce the potential for rubs on aft end compressor blades. In addition to the GER 3620 guidelines, the following recommendations would also help minimize aft end rubs and tip loss occurrence.
Keep enclosure doors closed during startup, shutdown and normal operation.
Be aware that restarting the gas turbine between two (2) and eight (8) hours following a shutdown or trip will cause the clearances in the aft end to decrease. If the unit operates this way now or has in the past, there is a potential for this clearance closure to cause aft end tip rubs. As a result, the area should be included in the yearly borescope inspections.
• Eliminate any potential pipe leaks that may cause quenching of the gas turbine compressor discharge casing.
Ensure vent fans and exhaust fans to the gas turbine enclosure are functioning properly such that no local forced convection is taking place at or near the compressor discharge casing.
Integrate the inspection for aft end compressor rubs with your yearly scheduled borescope inspection per GER 3620. Observe rotor blade stages 13 through 17 and look for mushroomed material (see Figure 3), bluing at the blade tip, and / or markings in the casing area.

Mushrooming Material Tip

If rubs or tip loss do occur, blending to increase clearances can be performed at Major Inspections (MI) or when the Compressor Discharge Casing (CDC) is removed. During repairs, clearances of rotor blades can be increased radially by tip grinding and polishing, and tip corners repaired by blade blending. Typically, 20 mils radially of material can be removed to both increase clearance and remove heat affected and rolled over material.
Following this operation, a penetrant inspection must be performed to ensure no tip cracks are present. If the CDC is removed prior to the major inspection, clearances can also be increased to eliminate the potential for tip rubs should the customer desire.
